2acc5f3263.q: How did Jesse Cole transform the Gastonia Grizzlies from losing $150,000 annually to becoming fourth in the country in attendance?
2acc5f3263.a: Cole realized at age 23 as GM of a team with only 200 fans and $268 in the bank that they could never compete on talent alone, so he began studying P.T. Barnum, Walt Disney, and entertainment figures to make the games more about entertainment than baseball. He experimented for 10 years with grandma beauty pageants, flatulence fun nights, salute to underwear nights, and having players dance during games. This eventually climbed them to fourth in the country in attendance, made the team profitable, and sold out games, though they only received one media story during that decade.
2acc5f3263.e: Building the Savannah Bananas (with Jesse Cole, Founder and Owner)

4c17688d02.q: What happened when the Savannah Bananas launched and why did Jesse Cole sell his house within three months?
4c17688d02.a: The Bananas launched on October 4-5, 2015, into complete rejection from the community that had just lost their official minor league team to Columbia, South Carolina. Within three months, Cole had sold only a handful of tickets despite hosting a free launch event. By January 15, 2016, they had overdrafted their account and were completely out of money, forcing Cole and his wife Emily to sell their house in Gastonia, empty their savings account, and move into a garage-turned-studio in Savannah where they slept on a twin airbed and grocery shopped with just $30 per week.
4c17688d02.e: Building the Savannah Bananas (with Jesse Cole, Founder and Owner)

e10aefaee8.q: Why did the Savannah Bananas choose the name 'Bananas' after running a naming contest?
e10aefaee8.a: After receiving a thousand generic naming suggestions including spirits, ports, and anchors, a 62-year-old nurse named Lynn Moses suggested 'Bananas.' Cole and his team had already been thinking about the name and had developed complementary concepts including a senior citizen dance team called the Banana Nanas, a male cheerleading team called the Mananas, and a mascot named Split. Though the community initially criticized the name heavily and even booed Cole and his staff at Savannah's St. Patrick's Day parade, Cole believed the name and logo were bold enough to work and could not be criticized once properly executed.
e10aefaee8.e: Building the Savannah Bananas (with Jesse Cole, Founder and Owner)

51b1c950e9.q: What is the Savannah Bananas' current business scale and ticket pricing model?
51b1c950e9.a: The Savannah Bananas sold one million tickets last year and two million tickets the current year, with an additional 3.2 million person waiting list. Tickets are priced at approximately $35 per game with unlimited food and drinks included and no hidden fees. The team has over 15 million followers on social media, including more TikTok followers than every MLB team combined.
51b1c950e9.e: Building the Savannah Bananas (with Jesse Cole, Founder and Owner)

745dc3694c.q: What are the main rules of Banana Ball that differentiate it from traditional baseball?
745dc3694c.a: Banana Ball features a man on stilts performing during games, choreographed dances by players, and approximately 15 unique rules including: if a fan catches your foul ball you are out, if you bunt you are ejected, and various other modifications to traditional baseball gameplay designed to create entertainment-focused play.
745dc3694c.e: Building the Savannah Bananas (with Jesse Cole, Founder and Owner)

f13add4dff.q: What financial deal did the Savannah Bananas negotiate to operate at the historic Grayson Stadium?
f13add4dff.a: The Savannah Bananas convinced the city of Savannah to lease them the historic Grayson Stadium (a 1926 ballpark where Babe Ruth, Hank Aaron, and Jackie Robinson played) for $20,000 per year after the previous minor league team demanded a $38 million new stadium and left for Columbia, South Carolina. Cole used the precedent from his Gastonia team to convince the city to support a college summer team at this legacy venue.
f13add4dff.e: Building the Savannah Bananas (with Jesse Cole, Founder and Owner)

a274b22bae.q: What mental framework should a technology leader use to evaluate emerging AI capabilities?
a274b22bae.a: Tobi Lütke spends significant time interviewing new AI models to understand their capabilities, building personal test harnesses called 'evals' — essentially folders of prompts with expected and judged results that he runs against every new model to determine where the edges are and whether the technology has crossed significant thresholds. He compares this approach to how machine learning experts have traditionally worked, using batch jobs that try the same things repeatedly and judge results, similar to how unit tests revolutionized software development in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
a274b22bae.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)

f9555169bd.q: How has the cost and nature of software production changed with AI-generated code?
f9555169bd.a: Code used to be the most expensive thing to produce, but now with AI, a lot of code that glues together infrastructure can be treated as a first draft rather than a final product. This is extremely healthy because it allows rapid iteration, though really good code for critical systems still requires the same careful approach as before.
f9555169bd.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)

5e2eb14a1e.q: What role should platform abstractions play in software architecture?
5e2eb14a1e.a: Good abstractions should raise the floor — making a minimum quality level accessible — without lowering the ceiling that limits how good something can ultimately become. Lossy abstractions that pretend a system is simpler than it actually is constrain what builders can create on top; operating systems like Windows, Linux, and OS X are examples of abstractions that raise the floor significantly without constraining the ceiling, a property Lütke believes e-commerce platforms should also achieve.
5e2eb14a1e.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)

892521d257.q: How can AI help merchants achieve their vision for their businesses?
892521d257.a: Shopify is increasingly asking merchants what their goals are and using AI to help them achieve them. With AI, the company can now action previously inactionable information — for example, a rug company tripled their European sales by using AI tools to change product images from Malibu beach houses to Parisian apartments without a new photo shoot, something that would have been technically impossible three years ago but is now straightforward.
892521d257.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)

bd84b05ea9.q: Why did the tech community largely overlook the moment AI systems passed the Turing test?
bd84b05ea9.a: The Turing test was passed by AI systems like GPT-3.5 without widespread celebration or recognition because the entire tech community was focused on whether this represented a path to Artificial General Intelligence rather than appreciating the achievement itself. Humans are incredibly good at moving the goalpost and adjusting to new circumstances; we normalize extraordinary technologies remarkably quickly, and the community's attention had already shifted to the next future milestone.
bd84b05ea9.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)

8e466e532e.q: What is the current state of consumer AR and VR technology adoption?
8e466e532e.a: Augmented reality glasses can be purchased next week, and VR devices like Meta Quest are available at approximately $299 and widely used for applications ranging from fitness workouts to racing simulator preparation. These technologies have folded into the ambient world and are taken for granted, despite being remarkable devices that were once purely speculative.
8e466e532e.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)

42daf3010a.q: How should leaders design for technological futures they cannot fully predict?
42daf3010a.a: Leaders should live in everyone else's relative future by staying on the cutting edge of emerging technologies and design choices — for example, by running beta software and adopting new UI paradigms early. This approach ensures that products are designed for the device and context as it will be experienced by users in the future, not as it exists today, which is the biggest job a CEO can do for their company and customers.
42daf3010a.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)

169317be8a.q: How did a reporter launch a daily email newsletter in 2001, over 15 years before Substack emerged?
169317be8a.a: Andrew Ross Sorkin started DealBook in 2001 after returning to New York from London, where he was covering mergers and acquisitions. Frustrated that Wall Street professionals told him they read the Wall Street Journal instead of the New York Times, he conceived of sending a daily report directly to their inboxes. The original idea was to bypass the physical paper and link readers to relevant stories, including competitors' coverage and SEC filings. Within a couple of months, the newsletter caught fire, with people requesting subscriptions and CEOs asking to have it faxed to their offices.
169317be8a.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

0e531f7012.q: What was the first advertiser for DealBook when it launched?
0e531f7012.a: The original advertiser for DealBook was Brooks Brothers. Sorkin notes that while Brooks Brothers is still in business today, they have gone in and out of business a couple of times since then.
0e531f7012.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

bbe407319a.q: How does a media professional manage multiple demanding roles simultaneously across television, newsletters, and books?
bbe407319a.a: Andrew Ross Sorkin's day typically begins around 4:30 in the morning, when he wakes up and checks email and messages under the covers. He spends about an hour before Squawk Box starts (which runs from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. Eastern) making tweaks to the DealBook newsletter. The newsletter team, which has grown significantly, includes colleagues like Michael Dillamer who has been with him for about 20 years, and Bernard Warner working overnight from Italy. Sorkin notes that all these projects inform each other in interesting ways, allowing him to have the best of both worlds.
bbe407319a.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

470cacac8c.q: How should journalists approach sources who have mixed or ulterior motives for sharing information?
470cacac8c.a: Sorkin believes every source has some motivation for talking, and it is typically self-interested. Rather than worrying about their ultimate incentives, he focuses on confirming information from two, three, or four different sources or obtaining documentation. He notes that some of the best sources have completely terrible and ulterior motives—people wanting to screw someone else over, board members trying to stop or advance deals, or bankers who have lost business to competitors and want to leak information.
470cacac8c.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

24b5fd099e.q: What is the role of junior employees and 'jilted' insiders in uncovering major business stories?
24b5fd099e.a: Great stories often start at very junior levels, not just with senior people. Sorkin identifies what he calls the 'jilted somebody'—someone who lost an auction, was passed over for business by a competitor, or spent years cultivating a client relationship only to see Goldman Sachs win the account instead. These individuals have no remaining stake in the game except the ability to upset the situation, making them more inclined to leak information or provide insights to reporters.
24b5fd099e.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

ec3fa9d7b0.q: What was the initial market size expectation for DealBook compared to its actual growth?
ec3fa9d7b0.a: When launching DealBook during the dot-com bust, the New York Times thought the total addressable market was 30,000 free subscribers. Today, DealBook has grown to over one million subscribers, far exceeding initial projections.
ec3fa9d7b0.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

5831e8daee.q: How did Andrew Ross Sorkin's first assignment at the New York Times happen?
5831e8daee.a: In 1995, Sorkin was coming to the New York Times office with a visitor pass, wearing a suit and tie, and performing clerical tasks like Xeroxing and stapling. An editor who had no idea how old he was overheard him talking about the Internet and assigned him a story to write. His first published piece was about the noise that modems make, explaining to readers that the noise was the two modems 'talking to each other' over a phone line.
5831e8daee.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

5befe269b3.q: What was Andrew Ross Sorkin's business venture before joining the New York Times full-time?
5befe269b3.a: At age 15, Sorkin created Sports Page Magazine at Scarsdale High School, which published sports journalism written by high school students and targeted young male readers through advertising. The magazines were distributed across the country inside high schools. He spent about a year successfully selling ads at $900 to $1,200 per full-page ad, but the venture ultimately failed by age 18 due to operational mistakes—including expensive Federal Express shipping for mailings and miscalculating printing costs with the same printer that worked with Wired magazine.
5befe269b3.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

22949a1381.q: Why did Plaid terminate the Visa acquisition deal for $5.3 billion?
22949a1381.a: Plaid terminated the deal in January 2021 because the DOJ signaled they were going to sue to block the acquisition. While Zach Perret believed Plaid would have won the lawsuit, he estimated it would have taken two years to close the deal, which would have locked in a $5 billion price despite significant business growth and improved prospects. At that point, Perret believed Plaid was worth more independently, and many of the original concerns that had motivated selling were gone.
22949a1381.e: Undoing a $5 Billion Acquisition and Building a Durable Standalone Plaid (with Plaid CEO Zach Perret)

cfc856aa31.q: How did Plaid's business perform during the pending Visa acquisition in 2020?
cfc856aa31.a: Plaid's business boomed during the acquisition period. Consumers stuck at home realized they still needed financial services, driving heavy usage of Plaid's products. Money was free and startups were being founded everywhere—all of Plaid's customers got funded, crypto was taking off with many on-ramps, and neobanks were proliferating. This fintech boom created a great tailwind for growth, allowing Plaid to continue expanding rapidly despite the pending deal.
cfc856aa31.e: Undoing a $5 Billion Acquisition and Building a Durable Standalone Plaid (with Plaid CEO Zach Perret)

86ff70d36a.q: What was Plaid's valuation trajectory after walking away from the Visa deal?
86ff70d36a.a: After terminating the Visa deal in January 2021 at $5 billion, Plaid raised the Altimeter round in April 2021 at approximately $13.5 billion valuation. A later fundraising round valued the company at $6 billion. Zach Perret was able to offer employees secondary sales at the higher $13.5 billion valuation, allowing them to take something off the table after the disappointing Visa deal cancellation.
86ff70d36a.e: Undoing a $5 Billion Acquisition and Building a Durable Standalone Plaid (with Plaid CEO Zach Perret)

4a4a03c557.q: How did Scott Cook's advice influence Zach Perret's decision on the Visa acquisition?
4a4a03c557.a: Scott Cook, founder of Intuit, emailed Zach Perret the day after the Visa acquisition was announced, congratulating him but warning that if the acquisition failed, Perret would be fine and might actually be great. Cook shared that the best thing that happened to him was when Microsoft's acquisition of Intuit was blocked for antitrust, after which Intuit became a multi-hundred billion dollar company. This advice planted a seed in Perret's mind and proved prescient when he decided to walk away from the Visa deal.
4a4a03c557.e: Undoing a $5 Billion Acquisition and Building a Durable Standalone Plaid (with Plaid CEO Zach Perret)

f7fb3fbeef.q: What was Plaid's original business model before pivoting to the bank linking API?
f7fb3fbeef.a: Plaid initially built consumer financial products including mobile budgeting tools and spending recommendations, similar to personal financial management tools. The company discovered that nobody wanted to use an app that told them to spend less money. After a conversation with the head of engineering at Venmo, who expressed interest in licensing Plaid's back-end infrastructure, the founders pivoted to focus exclusively on building an API for bank accounts rather than consumer-facing applications.
f7fb3fbeef.e: Undoing a $5 Billion Acquisition and Building a Durable Standalone Plaid (with Plaid CEO Zach Perret)

f61673fc50.q: Were Plaid and Visa direct competitors in the payments market?
f61673fc50.a: Plaid and Visa were not direct competitors. While the DOJ alleged that Visa was a monopolist and that buying Plaid was a path to expand that monopoly, Zach Perret clarifies they did not compete on any specific product. Plaid was building an API for bank account linking and enabling new payment methods, while Visa was the historical credit card payment network. In a meta sense, you could say Plaid represented the new financial system competing against Visa's existing system, but they did not compete on individual products or transactions.
f61673fc50.e: Undoing a $5 Billion Acquisition and Building a Durable Standalone Plaid (with Plaid CEO Zach Perret)
